record.paper_title: Some open questions in axion theory
record.original_question: After a QCD axion is discovered, how can one determine its quantized photon coupling with enough precision to test ultraviolet predictions such as the Grand Unified Theory value E/N = 8/3, given that haloscope measurements determine a rate proportional to g_aγγ^2 ρ_DM and therefore are degenerate with the poorly known local dark-matter density? In particular, can one identify an axion dark-matter sub-component whose local density can be predicted more accurately than the total local dark-matter density?

evidence.quote: However, the rate measures a combination g2 aγγρDM of the coupling and the local DM density. Unfortunately the local DM density is not known very precisely at the moment, and it will be challenging to pin it down to a few %, even assuming that axion DM makes up the entire DM density. It will be interesting to investigate if it would be possible to identify a sub-component of DM with a more accurate local density prediction.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. A QCD axion is a hypothetical pseudoscalar particle a coupled to photons through the Lagrangian term

  L_aγγ = (1/4) g_aγγ a F_{μν} \tilde F^{μν},

where the dimensionless model coupling is parameterized by the anomaly ratio E/N via

  g_aγγ = (α/2π f_a) (E/N − 1.92),

with α the fine-structure constant and f_a the axion decay constant. UV completions predict definite rational values of E/N; for example, the canonical grand-unified value is E/N = 8/3.

A resonant cavity ("haloscope") searching for axion dark matter measures a power that, on resonance, is proportional to

  P_signal ∝ g_aγγ^2 · ρ_a,local,

where ρ_a,local is the local mass density of the axion component of dark matter. Hence a haloscope detection determines only the product g_aγγ^2 ρ_a,local. The total local dark matter density ρ_DM,local is currently known only to roughly 10–50% accuracy, and even under the assumption ρ_a,local = ρ_DM,local this prevents extracting g_aγγ (and therefore E/N) to the precision needed to discriminate between competing UV completions.

Problem. Devise a strategy, after the discovery of a QCD axion, to determine the photon coupling g_aγγ (equivalently the anomaly coefficient E/N) with precision sufficient to distinguish among discrete UV predictions such as E/N = 8/3. In particular:

(a) Identify a sub-component of cold dark matter (for instance, a population of axion miniclusters, axion stars, a coherent stream, or a tidal substructure) whose local mass density ρ_sub,local can be predicted theoretically with substantially better fractional accuracy than the total local dark matter density ρ_DM,local.

(b) Show how an observable signature of this sub-component (e.g. transient haloscope events, gravitational microlensing, encounter rates) can be combined with a standard haloscope rate measurement to break the degeneracy between g_aγγ^2 and ρ_a,local and to extract g_aγγ at the few-percent level.

Alternatively, propose an independent measurement of g_aγγ that does not rely on the local dark matter density (e.g. light-shining-through-walls, helioscope, or astrophysical determinations) and quantify the achievable precision on E/N.
artifact.status_search_result: The coupling–density degeneracy in haloscope axion searches remains an active research problem. Recent proposals (axion miniclusters as a tagged sub-component, ultimate light-shining-through-walls experiments, and combinations with helioscopes) have explored ways to break the degeneracy, but no consensus method has been established that achieves percent-level determination of g_aγγ sufficient to discriminate UV predictions such as E/N = 8/3. The question is therefore still open, with partial progress in several directions.

status_evidence.title: Using Axion Miniclusters to Disentangle the Axion-photon Coupling and the Dark Matter Density
status_evidence.snippet: Establishing the axion as the dark matter particle after a haloscope discovery typically requires follow-up experiments to break the degeneracy between the axion's coupling to photons and its local dark matter abundance.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work proposes miniclusters as a sub-component whose encounter statistics help disentangle g_aγγ from ρ_DM,local; the broader problem of percent-level coupling extraction remains open.

status_evidence.title: Ultimate light-shining-through-a-wall experiments to establish QCD axions as the dominant form of dark matter
status_evidence.snippet: An independent measurement of the coupling, in combination with the haloscope measurement, determines the local axion fraction.
status_evidence.claim: Independent LSW measurements of g_aγγ are proposed as a complementary route, indicating the problem is still being actively investigated.

status_evidence.title: Limits on axion–photon coupling or on local axion density: Dependence on models of the Milky Way's dark halo
status_evidence.snippet: Limits are dependent upon the assumption of a halo model.
status_evidence.claim: Existing haloscope limits/measurements remain entangled with uncertain halo modeling.
